question_text: What does a runway number physically represent?

options.text: The runway magnetic compass heading rounded to the nearest 10 degrees, with the last zero dropped.
The runway length in hundreds of feet.
The runway assigned sequence number at the airport.

explanation_correct: A runway number is its magnetic heading divided by 10. Runway 27 = approximately 270 degrees magnetic.

explanation_distractors.B: Runway numbers have nothing to do with length.
explanation_distractors.C: Runway numbers are not arbitrary sequence numbers.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Ch. 10

question_text: If you are taking off on Runway 9, what magnetic direction are you heading?

options.text: East (090 degrees magnetic).
West (270 degrees magnetic).
North (360 degrees magnetic).

explanation_correct: Runway 9 times 10 equals 090 degrees, which is due East.

explanation_distractors.B: 270 degrees is Runway 27, the opposite end.
explanation_distractors.C: 360 degrees is Runway 36.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Ch. 10

question_text: What is the math rule to find the opposite end of any runway?

options.text: Add or subtract 18 (representing a 180-degree turnaround).
Multiply the runway number by 2.
Add 9 to the runway number.

explanation_correct: Adding or subtracting 18 gives the opposite runway. Runway 13 plus 18 equals Runway 31.

explanation_distractors.B: Multiplying by 2 does not work for this calculation.
explanation_distractors.C: Adding 9 gives a 90-degree difference, not 180 degrees.

question_text: If an aircraft lands on Runway 13, what runway number is painted on the opposite end?

options.text: Runway 31.
Runway 22.
Runway 4.

explanation_correct: 13 plus 18 equals 31. The opposite end of Runway 13 is Runway 31 (130 degrees plus 180 degrees equals 310 degrees).

explanation_distractors.B: Runway 22 is the opposite of Runway 4, not Runway 13.
explanation_distractors.C: Runway 4 is 040 degrees magnetic. The opposite of 13 is 31.

question_text: Runway numbers are based on which type of north?

options.text: Magnetic north.
True north.
Grid north.

explanation_correct: Runway numbers are based on magnetic north because pilots navigate using magnetic compasses.

explanation_distractors.B: True north is used on some maps but not for runway numbering.
explanation_distractors.C: Grid north is used in military operations.

question_text: In relation to the wind, which direction do manned aircraft normally take off and land?

options.text: Into the wind. A headwind gives the best lift and shortest runway distance.
With the wind. A tailwind increases ground speed.
Perpendicular to the wind. A crosswind provides stability.

explanation_correct: Aircraft take off and land into the wind. A headwind provides additional airflow over the wings, reducing the ground distance needed.

explanation_distractors.B: A tailwind increases ground speed but reduces lift effectiveness, requiring more runway.
explanation_distractors.C: A crosswind creates lateral drift and is not preferred for takeoff or landing.

question_text: If the wind is blowing heavily from the South (180 degrees), which runway is an aircraft most likely to use: Runway 18 or Runway 36?

options.text: Runway 18 — flying into the 180-degree wind.
Runway 36 — flying away from the wind.
Either runway, because wind direction does not matter.

explanation_correct: Runway 18 means flying a heading of 180 degrees (South). Since the wind is from the South, the aircraft flies into the headwind for optimal performance.

explanation_distractors.B: Runway 36 heads North (360 degrees). With a south wind that would be a tailwind, which is undesirable.
explanation_distractors.C: Wind direction is critical for determining the active runway.

question_text: If the wind is blowing from the West (270 degrees), which runway is active: Runway 9 or Runway 27?

options.text: Runway 27 — flying into the 270-degree wind.
Runway 9 — flying east away from the wind.
Both runways are equally usable.

explanation_correct: Runway 27 means heading 270 degrees (West). With the wind from the West the aircraft flies directly into the headwind.

explanation_distractors.B: Runway 9 heads East (090 degrees). With wind from the West that would be a tailwind.
explanation_distractors.C: Pilots choose the runway that provides the most headwind component.

question_text: What is the standard turn direction for an airport traffic pattern?

options.text: Left turns, unless marked RP on the sectional chart for Right Pattern.
Right turns at all airports.
Alternating left and right turns.

explanation_correct: The standard traffic pattern uses left turns. Right traffic is used only when specifically designated by RP on the sectional chart or Airport Facility Directory.

explanation_distractors.B: Right turns are non-standard and only used when specifically designated.
explanation_distractors.C: Traffic patterns use consistent turn directions, not alternating.

question_text: What does the Upwind leg of a traffic pattern mean?

options.text: The flight path parallel to the landing runway, flying in the same direction as landing.
The turn from base to final approach.
The flight path perpendicular to the runway.

explanation_correct: The upwind leg is parallel to the runway in the direction of takeoff and landing. An aircraft flies it just after takeoff before turning crosswind.

explanation_distractors.B: The turn from base to final is not the upwind leg.
explanation_distractors.C: A perpendicular path would be the crosswind or base leg.

question_text: What does the Downwind leg of a traffic pattern mean?

options.text: The flight path parallel to the landing runway, flying in the opposite direction of landing.
The final straight-in approach to the runway.
The climb-out segment after takeoff.

explanation_correct: The downwind leg is flown parallel to the runway but in the opposite direction of the landing heading. For Runway 27 (heading 270 degrees), the downwind heading is 090 degrees.

explanation_distractors.B: The final approach is the last segment aligned with the runway, not the downwind.
explanation_distractors.C: The climb-out after takeoff is the upwind or departure leg.

question_text: If an aircraft is on the Left Downwind for Runway 27, what compass heading is the aircraft currently flying?

options.text: 090 degrees (East).
270 degrees (West).
180 degrees (South).

explanation_correct: Downwind is the opposite of the landing heading. Runway 27 equals 270 degrees. The opposite of 270 degrees is 090 degrees (East).

explanation_distractors.B: 270 degrees is the landing heading for Runway 27, not the downwind heading.
explanation_distractors.C: 180 degrees would be a perpendicular heading, not the downwind for Runway 27.

question_text: If an aircraft is on the Left Downwind for Runway 18, where is the aircraft located in relation to the runway?

options.text: East of the runway, flying North.
West of the runway, flying South.
North of the runway, flying East.

explanation_correct: Left downwind for Runway 18 (heading South 180 degrees): left turns put the pattern to the east. The aircraft flies North (opposite of 180 degrees) on the east side of the runway.

explanation_distractors.B: West is where a right pattern would be. Standard left turns put it east.
explanation_distractors.C: North of the runway with an east heading would be the base leg.

question_text: What is the Base leg of a traffic pattern?

options.text: The short perpendicular flight path where the aircraft transitions from downwind to final approach.
The initial climb-out leg after takeoff.
The leg parallel to the runway flown in the landing direction.

explanation_correct: The base leg is a short perpendicular segment connecting the downwind leg to the final approach. The aircraft descends and turns to align with the runway.

explanation_distractors.B: The climb-out after takeoff is the upwind or departure leg.
explanation_distractors.C: A leg parallel to the runway in the landing direction is the upwind leg.

question_text: What is the Final Approach leg?

options.text: The last straight segment where the aircraft is lined up with the runway centerline to land.
The segment where the aircraft circles the airport before landing.
The climbout after a touch-and-go landing.

explanation_correct: The final approach is the last straight-line segment aligned with the runway centerline, during which the aircraft descends to land.

explanation_distractors.B: Circling the airport is part of the pattern, not the final approach specifically.
explanation_distractors.C: A climbout after a touch-and-go is the upwind or departure leg.

question_text: If an aircraft announces it is on Final for Runway 22, what heading is it flying?

options.text: 220 degrees magnetic.
040 degrees magnetic.
180 degrees magnetic.

explanation_correct: On final the aircraft is aligned with the runway heading. Runway 22 equals 220 degrees magnetic.

explanation_distractors.B: 040 degrees is Runway 4, the opposite end of Runway 22.
explanation_distractors.C: 180 degrees is Runway 18, not Runway 22.

explanation_distractors.B: 010/190 degrees is Runway 1/19, a different runway.
explanation_distractors.C: 280 degrees is the heading for Runway 28 (the opposite end).

explanation_distractors.B: Southwest and flying toward the runway sounds like a base or final leg, not downwind.
explanation_distractors.C: Aircraft in the traffic pattern are offset from the runway, not directly over it.

question_text: What is the standard traffic pattern altitude (TPA) for most propeller-driven aircraft?

options.text: 1,000 ft AGL unless otherwise published.
500 ft AGL.
1,500 ft AGL.

explanation_correct: The standard TPA is 1,000 ft AGL for propeller aircraft unless otherwise published for the specific airport. Drone pilots should stay aware of aircraft at this altitude.

explanation_distractors.B: 500 ft AGL is below the standard pattern altitude.
explanation_distractors.C: 1,500 ft AGL is above the standard pattern altitude for propeller aircraft.
